terms.grammar: genitive of corpus, after its noun
evidence: Cic. Cael. 39: in labōre corporis atque in animī contentiōne
terms.comment: Latin says “of the body”: physical strength is vīrēs corporis, physical pain dolor corporis, physical exercise exercitātiō corporis or simply exercitātiō (see exercise). Against the mind it is corpus and animus: corpore senex, old in body (Cic. Sen. 38).

terms.gloss: of the body; made of flesh
evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.41: ignis corporeus, the body’s heat (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Rare in prose (Lewis & Short: chiefly Lucretius); its usual sense is material, having a body (see physical, material).
Post-Augustan, most often in the jurists (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: nec vērō corporī sōlum subveniendum est, sed mentī atque animō multō magis
phrases.english: and it is not only the body that needs help, but the mind and spirit much more

phrases.latin: omnemque vītae suae cursum in labōre corporis atque in animī contentiōne cōnficeret
phrases.english: and spent his whole life in physical toil and mental effort
